abstract.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), the most aggressive primary brain tumor, demonstrates persistent resistance to immunotherapy due to its profoundly immunosuppressive microenvironment and markedly limited T cell infiltration. In this context, we engineered a STING agonist–incorporated prodrug hydrogel that orchestrates dual activation of innate and adaptive immunity to prevent postoperative GBM recurrence. We found that this in situ–forming hydrogel integrates seamlessly with tumor resection procedures, serves as a drug depot for sustained tumoral releases of therapeutic agents, and thus reprograms the tumor microenvironment by promoting M1 macrophage polarization, suppressing regulatory T cell activity, and enhancing cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration, thereby establishing a robust antitumor immune response. As a postoperative adjuvant therapy, the hydrogel effectively inhibits orthotopic GBM recurrence and extends animal survival while establishing durable immune memory against tumor rechallenge. Our findings demonstrate the translational potential of immunologically engineered hydrogels for STING-activated immunotherapy in preventing postresection GBM recurrence.
A STING agonist–incorporated prodrug hydrogel activates innate and adaptive immunity to prevent GBM recurrence postresection.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) is recognized as the highly aggressive and treatment-refractory primary malignant brain tumor (1, 2). Despite comprehensive treatment involving maximal surgical resection followed by adjuvant radiotherapy and chemotherapy, more than two-thirds of GBM cases experience peri-cavitary recurrence (3–5), highlighting the urgent need for more effective therapeutic strategies. Although immunotherapy has revolutionized treatment for several advanced cancers, brain tumors remain a notable exception to this therapeutic progress (6–8). Through the analysis of Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets, we identified distinct gene expression profiles in GBM compared to those in normal tissues (fig. S1). Notably, we observed up-regulated genes were significantly enriched in pathways associated with negative regulation of both innate and adaptive immune responses (Fig. 1, A and B). Immune profiling demonstrated predominant tissue-resident macrophages and limited adaptive immune cells in GBM (GSM397636) relative to normal tissue (GSE397658) (Fig. 1C). Specifically, GBM tissues exhibited abundant immunosuppressive populations [such as M2 macrophages and regulatory T (Treg) cells] but were deficient in CD8+ T cells (Fig. 1, D to F), fostering an immunosuppressive microenvironment that promotes tumor progression and recurrence (9–12). These findings suggest that modulating immunosuppressive cell depletion while enhancing CD8+ T cell infiltration may restore antitumor immunity and prevent postoperative recurrence.

sec.p: Emerging evidence indicates that stimulator of interferon genes (STING) pathway activation potently enhances both innate and adaptive immune responses within the tumor microenvironment (TME) (13). Mechanistically, STING activation drives the phenotypic switch of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) to the M1 subtype, thereby reducing the infiltration of immunosuppressive cells into the TME (14, 15). Moreover, STING functions as a crucial cytoplasmic sensor that detects both endogenous and exogenous cytosolic DNA, subsequently initiating type I interferon (IFN) production through downstream signaling cascades (16–20). Accumulating evidence demonstrates that type I IFNs exert immunomodulatory functions by simultaneously inhibiting Treg cell activity and promoting dendritic cell (DC) maturation, thereby facilitating the activation and expansion of T cell populations. Notably, chemotherapeutic agents such as paclitaxel (PTX) function as potent immunogenic cell death (ICD) inducers, triggering tumor antigen release through tumor cell eradication. This process enhances GBM immunogenicity and promotes DC-mediated antigen presentation, ultimately facilitating the generation of antigen-specific T cell response (21–23). On the basis of these findings, we reason that the synergistic combination of PTX and STING agonist represents a promising therapeutic strategy to concurrently engage both innate and adaptive immune responses against GBM.

Despite their therapeutic potential, the clinical efficacy of intratumorally administered cyclic dinucleotide (CDN) STING agonists has been limited by poor bioavailability and off-target immune-related adverse effects (24), underscoring the critical need for developing efficient delivery systems to optimize their therapeutic effect. Our recent studies demonstrate that covalent conjugation of chemotherapeutic agents with self-assembling peptides facilitates their transformation into prodrug-based hydrogelator, enabling the formation of stable supramolecular filaments (25–27). By using a “drug-delivering-drug” strategy, this prodrug hydrogelator can be adapted for localized delivery of various therapeutic agents, facilitating synergistic combined therapy (28–30). Moreover, the rapid sol-gel transition of such prodrug hydrogelator under physiological conditions, enabling direct injection into the surgical resection cavity of GBM and subsequent in situ gel formation (31–34). On basis of these observations, we propose that the PTX-based prodrug hydrogelator could serve as an optimal delivery platform for localized administration of STING agonists in postresection brain tumor cavities, enabling maximal therapeutic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity.

Herein, we report the development of a PTX-based prodrug hydrogelator for localized combinatorial delivery of STING agonist [2′3′-c-di-AM (PS)2(Rp, Rp) (CDA)] and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF; to recruit DCs to the hydrogel matrix), demonstrating its potent ability to enhance innate-adaptive immune cross-talk and prevent postoperative GBM recurrence (Fig. 2). Our findings revealed that this dual-drug–loaded supramolecular prodrug filament rapidly forms a stable hydrogel upon intracavitary injection, serving as in situ drug depot for sustained, localized release of therapeutic agents into residual tumor microsatellites. GM-CSF facilitates the recruitment of immature DCs into the TME, where they capture tumor antigens released from PTX-induced ICD. These DCs, subsequently activated by CDA, process tumor antigens and promote the activation and tumor-directed migration of CD8+ T cells. Furthermore, CDA-mediated STING activation triggers M2-to-M1 macrophage repolarization and suppresses Treg cell function, thereby remodeling the immunosuppressive microenvironment. Ultimately, the synergistic enhancement of tumor-specific T cell infiltration and depletion of immunosuppressive cell populations significantly prevents GBM recurrence and prolongs animal survival.

sec.title: Characterization of the chemoimmunotherapeutic supramolecular hydrogel
sec.p: To develop prodrug hydrogelator, the PTX prodrug (PTX-iRGD) was synthesized via chemically conjugation of PTX to the iRGD peptide using the bio-reducible linker 4-(pyridin-2-yl-disulfanyl) butyrate (buSS) according to our previous report (35, 36). The detailed synthetic route and characterization of PTX-iRGD were shown in figs. S2 to S8. With the introduction of iRGD, the amphiphilic PTX prodrug in aqueous solution could spontaneously assemble into a supramolecular nanofilament defined as PF (Fig. 3A), which was subsequently converted into a solid hydrogel upon exposure to phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) (fig. S9). Negatively charged CDA and GM-CSF were coadsorbed onto the PF surface via electrostatic interactions at pH 7.4. This adsorption resulted in the formation of CDA+GM-CSF (CG)/PF complexes, accompanied by a decrease in Zeta potential value from 45.9 ± 1.23 mV (PF) to 36.87 ± 2.42 mV (CG/PF) (Fig. 3B). Both CDA and GM-CSF achieve 100% drug loading efficiency in the PF formulation. Notably, the CG/PF retained the “solution-to-hydrogel” transition property of the PF, as evidenced by a substantial increase in storage modulus (G′) upon addition of PBS (Fig. 3, C and D). To investigate the in vivo hydrogel transformation, the CG/PF solution was injected subcutaneously into C57BL/6 mice and underwent rapid sol-gel transition within 10 min, forming a solid hydrogel depot at the injection site (fig. S10). Therefore, the CG/PF was suitable for direct administration in the solution state and followed by gelation at the implantation site.

sec.title: CG/PF hydrogel serves as drug reservoir for sustained therapeutics release
sec.p: The release profiles of therapeutic agents from the hydrogel were determined in vitro. As depicted in Fig. 3E, the PTX-iRGD monomer exhibited linear release kinetics, achieving a cumulative release of 38.74% over 25 days. In response to elevated glutathione levels within tumor cells, the PTX-iRGD prodrug underwent bio-reducible cleavage through its disulfide-containing buSS linker, resulting in rapid release of 79.85% of the parent PTX within 24 hours (Fig. 3F). This result suggested a bioresponsive PTX-iRGD for the on-demand and controlled delivery of PTX into tumor cells. In addition, CG/PF hydrogel exhibited sustained release of immunotherapeutic agents CDA and GM-CSF, with cumulative release rates reaching 74.24 and 46.62% over 35 days, respectively (Fig. 3G). This sustained release profile highlights the potential of the CG/PF hydrogel as a drug reservoir for localized immunotherapy.

To demonstrate the prolonged immunotherapeutic agent release in vivo, C57BL/6 mice were treated subcutaneously with CG/PF or free CDA. As displayed in Fig. 3H, the fluorescence signal in the free CDA group was negligibly detectable at 10 days. In contrast, the fluorescence signal of the CG/PF group persisted for 20 days, with 23.87% of CDA remaining at the injection site (Fig. 3I), indicating that CG/PF could serve as a local drug depot and significantly prolong CDA release in vivo. Inspired by the ability of CG/PF to concentrate CDA at the desired site, we further investigated the retention behavior of CDA within the brain tissue. As demonstrated in Fig. 3J, the CG/PF hydrogel retained the CDA in the brain tissue and prevented its burst release. With the assistance of CG/PF hydrogel system, the release of CDA in the brain was sustained for up to 20 days (Fig. 3K), further suggesting that intracerebral injection of CG/PF retained the potential to prolong drug release and favored improve local treatment of GBM.

Because the PF can concentrate CDA at the desired site, we further evaluated the safety of CG/PF after intracranially injection in healthy mice. Notably, body weight was not affected by CG/PF treatment (fig. S11A). As shown in fig. S11B, hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining of major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney) revealed no signs of tissue damage or pathological changes. Similar to the healthy control group, serum biochemistry in mice treated with CG/PF showed no abnormalities (fig. S11C), supporting the biosafety of CG/PF. In addition, blood parameter analysis corroborated these results, with measured biochemical indicators comparable to those in the healthy control group (table S1). Collectively, these results demonstrated the favorable biosafety profile of CG/PF, supporting its potential for further antitumor research.

sec.title: CG/PF hydrogel attracts DCs to boost adaptive immunity
sec.p: The major hallmarks of ICD, including calreticulin (CRT) surface exposure and the release of soluble mediators such as high-mobility group box 1 protein (HMGB1) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP), are critical for DC activation and subsequent initiation of adaptive immunity (37, 38). To evaluate the ICD-inducing potential of PF, we investigated its effects on these biomarkers using flow cytometry and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). As shown in fig. S12A, compared to the PBS control, free PTX significantly enhanced CRT exposure on GL261 cells. The level of CRT-positive cells also increased in the PF-treated group, reaching levels comparable to that induced by free PTX. Similar trends were observed for the release of extracellular HMGB1 and ATP (fig. S12, B and C). These findings demonstrated that PF maintained ICD induction efficacy of PTX in GL261 cells, thereby potentially activating DCs.

To investigate whether this in situ–forming prodrug hydrogel could activate innate and adaptive immunity in vivo, flow cytometry was performed to evaluate its immunotherapeutic potential (figs. S13 to S15). Given the paucity of DCs in the GBM microenvironment, we hypothesized that the GM-CSF–incorporated CG/PF would recruit immature DCs and further process tumor-derived antigen induced by PTX to edit the adaptive immune response program, as shown in Fig. 4A. Consequently, the CG/PF significantly prompted the recruitment of CD45+ cells and DCs (identified as CD11c+MHC-II+ cells) into the TME, which was 1.68- and 1.87-fold higher than that of mice receiving normal saline (NS), respectively (Fig. 4, B to D). Compared to that in C/PF, the percentage of recruited DCs was 1.25-fold higher in the CG/PF group, underscoring GM-CSF’s role in DC recruitment. To further characterize DC subtypes, the conventional DC (cDC), plasmacytoid DC (pDC), and monocyte-derived DC (moDC) were analyzed by flow cytometry. As shown in Fig. 4D, the CG/PF group increased the percentage of cDC1, cDC2, moDC, and pDC in tumor tissues compared to the NS and PF groups. Furthermore, compared to the C/PF, CG/PF treatment exhibited a significant increase in cDC1, cDC2, and moDC, suggesting that GM-CSF enhanced the accumulation of these specific DC subsets. Subsequently, immature DCs underwent phenotypic maturation in response to ICD, facilitated by CDA-mediated activation of the STING pathway. The activation of STING pathway was further demonstrated by the type I IFN-α response (fig. S16) and the maturation of DCs. As shown in Fig. 4 (E and F), the population of activated CD80+ DCs was increased from 20.27% (PF) to 26.5% (CG/PF) and activated CD86+ DCs was increased from 11.87% (PF) to 27% (CG/PF), demonstrating that this supramolecular hydrogel CG/PF promoted the recruitment and activation of DCs, favoring adaptive immune surveillance.

sec.p: Mature DCs are considered to the bridge of the gap between innate and adaptive immunity, facilitating the interaction of DCs with naïve T cells in the lymph node and initiating the subsequent T cell immune response (15). As expected, immunization with CG/PF significantly increased the migratory DCs in the lymph node, which was 1.37-fold higher than that in the NS group (Fig. 4G). In addition, CG/PF increased the DC activation in the lymph node, in which the percentage of CD80+ DCs and CD86+ DCs was 1.34- and 1.71-fold higher than that of in the PF group, respectively (Fig. 4, H and I). These activated DCs provided costimulatory signals for the subsequent activation of CD3+CD4+ and CD3+CD8+ T cells in the lymph node. As demonstrated in Fig. 4 (J to L), CG/PF immunization increased the percentage of CD3+CD4+ and CD3+CD8+ T cells 2.26- and 1.63-fold, respectively, relative to the levels in NS-treated mice. Furthermore, with the introduction of adjuvants, the proportion of CD3+CD4+ T cells was increased from 26.87% (PF) to 37.77% (CG/PF) and that of CD3+CD8+ T cells was increased from 23.23% (PF) to 31.03% (CG/PF). Notably, CG/PF increased the percentage of antitumor IFN-γ+CD8+ T cells (25.47% versus 9.36%) and GzmB+CD8+ T cells (23.83% versus 7.04%) compared to the NS group (Fig. 4, M and N). These results suggested that CG/PF boosted the cross-talk between innate and adaptive immunity to activate a robust cellular immune response.

Furthermore, this CG/PF effectively activated the systemic immune potential as evidenced by the induction of immune cell activation in the spleen. Compared to the NS group, the CG/PF hydrogel increased the population of immunocytes such as CD3+CD4+ and CD3+CD8+ T cells, which were 1.35- and 1.27-fold greater than in the NS control group (fig. S17), respectively. Notably, with the assistance of STING agonist CDA, the proportion of CD3+CD4+ T cells was increased from 16.47% (PF) to 20.37% (CG/PF) and that of CD3+CD8+ T cells was increased from 11.77% (PF) to 14.2% (CG/PF), indicating that the systemic immune activation could be awakened by localized treatment with CG/PF. Moreover, the activated systemic immunity was further demonstrated by the up-regulation of cytokine levels (Fig. 4, O to R). The higher levels of cytokines including interleukin-2 (IL-2), IL-6, IFN-γ, and tumor necrosis factor–α (TNF-α) were secreted after CG/PF treatment, indicating the induction of a robust adaptive immune response by CG/PF. Collectively, the above results indicated that this supramolecular hydrogel CG/PF effectively elicited the systemic immune response and favored the inhibition of tumor progression.

sec.title: CG/PF hydrogel elicits an immunostimulatory microenvironment against orthotopic GBM
sec.p: Motivated by the aforementioned immune activation effects, the orthotopic GL261-Luc tumor model was established in female C57BL/6 mice to investigate the therapeutic efficacy of the CG/PF hydrogel (Fig. 5A). As displayed in Fig. 5B, the bioluminescence images in the NS group exhibited a rapid and aggressive tumor growth, whereas CG/PF significantly attenuated tumor growth kinetics. Consistently, the CG/PF group delayed the rate of tumor growth compared to PF (fig. S18), highlighting the critical role of combinatorial immunotherapy. Survival analysis further corroborated these findings, with CG/PF prolonging median survival to 59 days, compared to NS-treated mice (24 days) and PF-treated mice (36 days), respectively (Fig. 5C and table S2). This therapeutic superiority confirmed the enhanced antitumor potential of CG/PF over PF through synergistic immunotherapeutic modulation.

sec.p: Furthermore, the tumor-infiltrating immune cells were detected to assess whether CG/PF reshaped the GBM microenvironment. As shown in Fig. 5 (D and E), immunization with CG/PF significantly promoted the infiltration of CD3+CD8+ T cells into the GBM microenvironment, which was increased from 8.48 to 13.77% compared to that in the NS group. Similarly, the proportion of CD3+CD4+ T cells in the CG/PF group reached 18.37%, surpassing 12.13% in the NS group and 14.6% in the PF group (fig. S19). Additionally, CG/PF enhanced the antitumor immune response by reducing the presence of the unfavorable immunocyte Treg cells (Fig. 5F and fig. S20) while significantly elevating the CD8+ T cell/Treg cell (Fig. 5G) and CD4+ T cell/Treg cell ratios (Fig. 5H), which were indicated as vital parameters for robust immune activation performance.

Macrophages constitute the predominant immune population in the GBM tissue, typically polarizing toward the M2 phenotype to perpetuate the immunosuppressive milieu (39). CG/PF treatment induced a marked shift in macrophage polarization, significantly increasing the proportion of proinflammatory M1 macrophages (47.57% versus 20.3%) while reducing immunosuppressive M2 macrophages (21.7% versus 44.7%) compared to the NS group (Fig. 5, I to K). Accordingly, the CG/PF group exhibited a markedly elevated M1/M2 ratio, achieving a 4.89-fold increase compared to the NS control (Fig. 5L). This notable enhancement in proinflammatory/anti-inflammatory macrophage balance surpassed all other treatment groups, serving as a critical indicator of therapeutic immune remodeling. Thus, these findings confirmed that CG/PF drove M1 macrophage polarization, establishing a proinflammatory immune milieu critical for antitumor immunity.

sec.title: CG/PF hydrogel reprograms postresection inflammatory responses
sec.p: Considering that surgical resection remains the cornerstone of GBM treatment, the GL261-Luc tumor resection model was established to explore the CG/PF hydrogel as a postsurgical potential adjuvant therapy (Fig. 6A). Following orthotopic GBM implantation, postoperative model was allowed to establish after 8 days before performing microsurgical resection of the primary mass under stereotactic guidance (Fig. 6B). After tumor resection, the CG/PF solution was injected into the resection cavity, where it immediately transformed into the hydrogel state upon contact with biological fluid (Fig. 6C), indicating its ability to fill the cavity and enable sustained local drug delivery for residual tumor eradication. Quantitative bioluminescence imaging revealed residual tumor burden at 10% of the original signal intensity postresection (Fig. 6D). Although surgical intervention modestly extended median survival compared to untreated controls (32 days versus 24 days), all animals eventually succumbed to lethal tumor recurrence (Fig. 6E), highlighting the critical need for adjuvant strategies to prevent GBM relapse.

sec.p: To investigate the impact of surgical procedure and CG/PF hydrogel on inflammatory responses, we measured inflammatory cytokine levels (IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-10) in brain tissue and serum via ELISA. As shown in Fig. 6 (F to K), proinflammatory cytokines (IL-6 and TNF-α) in both compartments were transiently but significantly up-regulated on postoperative day 2 compared to presurgical baselines in control mice, followed by gradual decline over the observation period. CG/PF treatment sustained significantly elevated levels of these proinflammatory cytokines in brain and serum throughout the observation period. Specifically, at day 10 postresection, IL-6 and TNF-α levels in brain tissue were 3.18-fold and 2.89-fold higher, respectively, than those in time-matched controls. Conversely, the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 was significantly suppressed in CG/PF-treated mice relative to controls at all time points. These findings indicate that CG/PF reprograms postoperative immunity by persistently enhancing proinflammatory signaling while suppressing anti-inflammatory responses, which is distinct from the transient inflammation induced by surgery alone.

sec.title: CG/PF hydrogel prevents GBM recurrence postresection
sec.p: Recently, neoadjuvant immune checkpoint blockade therapy targeting the programmed cell death protein–1 and programmed cell death–ligand 1 (PD-1/PD-L1) pathway (40–42), which was administered before curative surgery in treatment-naïve patients, showed promising results in patients with GBM (43, 44). Therefore, to further improve the outcome of postoperative GBM treatment, the combined therapy of CG/PF and immune checkpoint blockade anti–PD-1 antibody (aPD-1) therapy was used to treat mice bearing GL261-Luc cells (Fig. 7A). Bioluminescence imaging confirmed that the orthotopic GL261-Luc tumor model was formed on day 8 postinoculation (Fig. 7B). After surgical tumor removal on day 9, bioluminescence imaging demonstrated a marked reduction in intracranial tumor signal. Notably, immunization with combined treatment of CG/PF and aPD-1, the mice showed negligible tumor growth and recurrence, whereas that of the NS control group accelerated tumor growth. The NS-treated mice all died within 38 days and showed a significantly reduced median survival time, as compared with the mice receiving PF (32 days versus 58 days) from table S3. With the introduction of immunotherapeutic agents, the mice treated with C/PF or CG/PF significantly inhibited tumor recurrence, with tumor progression significantly decreased compared to those of the control group, and both formulations concomitantly extended median postoperative survival. This combinatorial surgical-immunotherapeutic strategy established durable tumor control superior to treatment alone without surgical intervention (table S4). Notably, the CG/PF and aPD-1 treatment with surgical resection achieved 100% recurrence-free survival and all mice survived beyond 120 days (Fig. 7, C and D). Collectively, these results suggested that postoperative intracavitary implantation of CG/PF hydrogel with neoadjuvant therapy showed promise as a combined and effective treatment strategy for GBM.

sec.p: Furthermore, flow cytometric analysis revealed significant alterations in immune cell infiltration within postresection GBM microenvironment. Compared to the NS group, CG/PF-treated mice exhibited increased infiltration of DCs, CD3+CD8+ T cells, and M1 macrophages within tumor tissue (Fig. 7, E and F, and fig. S21). Notably, CG/PF combined with aPD-1 significantly increased the percentage of IFN-γ+CD8+ T cells (10.87% versus 1.62%) and GzmB+CD8+ T cells (8.62% versus 0.53%) compared to the NS group (Fig. 7, G and H). Concurrently, Treg cell and M2 macrophage proportion was markedly reduced in the CG/PF group (Fig. 7, I to L). When combined with CDA, CG/PF reprogrammed the immunosuppressive microenvironment versus the PF group, as evidenced by the reduced percentage of Treg cells (12.56% versus 19.17%), increased CD8+ T cell/Treg cell ratio (0.98 versus 0.43), reduced percentage of M2 macrophages (13.51% versus 28.9%), and increased M1/M2 ratio (2.32 versus 0.59). This immune remodeling, characterized by enhanced infiltration of antitumor effectors (DCs, effector CD8+ T cells, and M1 macrophages) alongside diminished infiltration of protumorigenic populations (M2 macrophages and Treg cells), demonstrates that CG/PF coordinately modulates both innate immunity (macrophage polarization and DC recruitment) and adaptive immunity (CD8+ T cell activation and Treg cell suppression) within the TME, potentially preventing postresection GBM recurrence.

sec.title: CG/PF hydrogel induces durable immunological memory against GBM rechallenge
sec.p: Given the robust immunostimulatory effect of CG/PF, we wondered whether the locally implanted CG/PF could induce an immune memory effect against tumor rechallenge. Accordingly, mice surviving ≥120 days in the CG/PF and CG/PF and aPD-1 groups were designated long-term survivors and rechallenged with GL261-Luc cells contralaterally. Naïve mice received equivalent primary inoculations on the same day as rechallenge controls (Fig. 8A). As shown in Fig. 8B, the bioluminescence signal in naïve mice exhibited a significant increase by day 21 postinoculation. In contrast, rechallenged mice in the CG/PF and CG/PF and aPD-1 groups showed inhibition of tumor progression, as evidenced by weaker bioluminescence signals in the brain area and confirmed by H&E staining, alongside extended survival (Fig. 8, C to E). The combined CG/PF and aPD-1 treatment achieved maximal tumor growth inhibition and significantly prolonged survival compared to controls, attributable to the blockade of immunosuppressive signals and the establishment of durable immune memory against tumor growth. Flow cytometry analysis elevated proportions of CD44+CD62L+ central memory T (Tcm) cells among CD4+ T cells (CD4+ Tcm cells) and CD8+ T cells (CD8+ Tcm cells) in the spleen. Specifically, CG/PF and aPD-1–treated mice showed increased CD4+ Tcm (23.23% versus 14.67%) and CD8+ Tcm (28.23% versus 17.4%) cells compared to the naïve control (Fig. 8, F and G). Furthermore, increased effector memory cells in CD4+ T cells (CD4+ Tem cells) and in CD8+ T cells (CD8+ Tem cells) were also observed in the combined therapy (Fig. 8, H and I). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that a single localized CG/PF hydrogel treatment, combined with neoadjuvant aPD-1 therapy, elicited a robust and enduring antitumor immunological memory response.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Surgical resection remains the primary treatment for most patients with GBM. However, residual neoplastic satellites inevitably lead to tumor recurrence (45, 46). This process is exacerbated by the infiltration of immunosuppressive cells (e.g., M2 macrophages and Treg cells) and the paucity of CD8+ T cells (21, 47), which are hallmarks of GBM and present a significant challenge to improving clinical outcomes. In our previous work, we developed a PTX-bearing supramolecular hydrogel for local delivery of anti-CD47 antibody (aCD47), demonstrating its efficacy against recurrent glioblastoma (48). We discovered that the PF hydrogel triggered TAM infiltration, which synergized with localized aCD47 to promote macrophage-mediated tumor cell phagocytosis while concurrently activating T cell–mediated antitumor immunity. However, recent immunological analysis revealed predominant enrichment of M2-polarized macrophages in gliomas (Fig. 1D), which establish an immunosuppressive GBM microenvironment and attenuate antitumor responses. Furthermore, analysis of GEO datasets from GBM samples showed significant enrichment of up-regulated genes in both innate immune pathways (characterized by M2 macrophage polarization and impaired DC recruitment) and adaptive immune pathways (marked by CD8+ T cell deficiency and regulatory T cell infiltration) (Fig. 1). This immunosuppressive profile underscores the necessity for a synergistic strategy targeting both immune arms.

As previously reported, activation of the STING signaling pathway drives the polarization of TAMs toward M1-type macrophages and attenuates Treg cell activity (49, 50). Furthermore, it promotes DC maturation, thereby facilitating the activation and expansion of T cell populations (51, 52). While natural CDNs are highly susceptible to degradation by phosphodiesterases and non-CDN STING agonists often exhibit unfavorable pharmacokinetics, synthetic CDNs such as CDA mitigate these limitations. Furthermore, CDA’s hydrophilic/anionic backbone enables nanostructure formulation through electrostatic interactions (53–55). CDA has demonstrated robust immune activation in GBM models (13). Leveraging these advantages, we used a PTX-based prodrug hydrogelator for the localized codelivery of the STING agonist CDA and GM-CSF, simultaneously activating both innate and adaptive immune responses against GBM. We observed that CG/PF attracted CD45+ cells (12.03% versus 7.17%) and DCs (9.22% versus 4.93%) into the tumor tissue compared to NS, the immunomodulatory advantage of the CG/PF was further elucidated by an increased population of CD80+ DCs and CD86+ DCs. These DCs, activated by CDA, processed tumor antigens and promoted the activation and tumor-directed migration of CD8+ T cells. Furthermore, CG/PF significantly up-regulated the M1/M2 ratios (2.21 versus 0.45) and reduced Treg cell population (12.8% versus 22.5%) compared to NS. Collectively, these results demonstrate that CG/PF reprograms the immunosuppressive GBM niche through coordinated innate-adaptive immunomodulation: reactivating innate immunity by macrophage repolarization and DC mobilization while reinvigorating adaptive immunity via enhanced CD8+ T cell infiltration and Treg cell suppression.

These findings established a compelling mechanistic basis for the enhanced therapeutic outcomes in GL261 GBM models. We found that CG/PF-treated mice exhibited significantly attenuated tumor progression (P < 0.01) and reduced tumor burden compared to PF monotherapy controls. Notably, the combination of CG/PF treatment with surgical resection achieved efficient tumor eradication, with 75% of treated mice maintaining tumor-free survival up to 120 days. This effect was attributed to the ability of CG/PF treatment to inhibit immunosuppressive cells (M2 macrophages and Treg cells) enrichment, and enhance CD8+ T cell infiltration, thus preventing GBM recurrence postresection. The therapeutic potential was further augmented through synergistic incorporation of immune checkpoint inhibitors, which not only enhanced local tumor control but also established systemic immunological memory, providing durable protection against tumor rechallenge. In contrast to conventional postsurgical chemotherapy approaches that target residual microsatellites (56), this rationally designed immunotherapeutic hydrogel platform, engineered to modulate the unique immunosuppressive TME of GBM, demonstrated superior efficacy in preventing postoperative recurrence through the induction of robust and durable antitumor immunity.

Distinct from conventional solid hydrogel implants (57, 58), this in situ–forming hydrogel system features a unique solution-to-gel transition, offering simplified administration. The injectable formulation enables precise deposition into the resection cavity, followed by rapid gelation that seamlessly integrates with standard surgical procedures, thereby optimizing treatment compliance for patients with GBM. Furthermore, the platform uses an innovative “drug delivery by drug” strategy for codelivering chemotherapeutic and immunotherapeutic agents. The supramolecular structure enables sustained CDA release over 20 days, achieved through stable complex formation with the PTX prodrug hydrogelator rather than relying on conventional physical entrapment (59), effectively minimizing drug loss. Notably, while previous attempts using high-dose STING agonists (100 nmol) demonstrated limited therapeutic efficacy in preclinical models (60), our low-dose approach (14.5 nmol) combined with the PTX prodrug hydrogelator delivery system achieved superior tumor regression and prevention of relapse. These benefits highlight the ability of prodrug hydrogelator platform to enhance STING agonist efficacy through optimized delivery.

In summary, we have developed a prodrug hydrogel system that activates the STING pathway to establish an immunostimulatory microenvironment, effectively combating GBM recurrence. This in situ–forming hydrogel seamlessly integrates with tumor resection procedures, functioning as a drug depot that continuously delivers therapeutic agents into the TME. The system induces macrophage polarization toward the M1 phenotype, suppresses Treg cell activity, and enhances cytotoxic T lymphocyte infiltration, collectively contributing to tumor eradication. Moreover, local hydrogel implantation establishes durable immunological memory, significantly inhibiting GBM progression and recurrence. Our results demonstrate that this immunologically engineered hydrogel system exhibits remarkable therapeutic potential and clinical advantages for preventing GBM recurrence postresection.

sec.title: Cells and animals
sec.p: GL261-Luc cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Gibco, Invitrogen) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum and G418 (100 μg/ml; Invitrogen). Six- to 8-week-old female C57BL/6 mice were purchased from Shanghai SLAC Laboratory Animal Co. Ltd. All experiments protocols were conducted in accordance with the Animal Ethics Committee of Shanghai Jiao Tong University [SYXK (Hu) 2018-0028].

sec.title: Preparation of CG/PF
sec.p: Amphiphilic PTX-iRGD was dissolved in deionized water and self-assembly into nanofilament, defined as PF. CDA and GM-CSF were then added to the PF solution and incubated at 37°C for 1 hour. Subsequently, the mixture was equilibrated at room temperature for a minimum of 24 hours to enable spontaneous self-assembly into CG/PF. The CG/PF was isolated and purified through repeated washing/centrifugation cycle to remove unbound components. Last, gelation was induced by supplementing the CG/PF solution with 10× PBS to induce ionic cross-linking, resulting in hydrogel formation.

sec.title: Solution-to-hydrogel transition
sec.p: Twenty microliters of 10× PBS was added to 180 μl of CG/PF solution in a clear glass vial, and the solution-to-hydrogel transformation was tested using the inversion method. The real-time gelation properties of CG/PF were further determined using a rheometer (DMAQ850, TA Instruments). The rheometer frequency was set to 10 Hz and 0.5% strain, 180 μl of the CG/PF solution was added to the rheometer tray to perform a time scan, and 20 μl of 10× PBS was added to the CG/PF solution using a syringe after 3 min. The gelation kinetics of CG/PF were monitored by tracking the changes in storage modulus (G′) and loss modulus (G″) over time.

sec.title: In vitro drug release from CG/PF hydrogel
sec.p: To prepare the CG/PF hydrogel, 180 μl of CG/PF solution was added to a 1.5-ml centrifuge tube, followed by the addition of 20 μl of 10× PBS. The release medium 1× PBS solution was added to the centrifuge tube, and release medium was sampled at the specified time points and replaced with fresh 1× PBS solution. Each sample was replicated three times. The cumulative release of PF and CDA was determined by HPLC, and the cumulative release of GM-CSF was detected by the GM-CSF ELISA Kit.

sec.title: In situ gelation
sec.p: The transition from solution to hydrogel in situ was observed by photography. CG/PF solution (100 μl) was injected subcutaneously into 6- to 8-week-old female C57BL/6 mice, and in situ hydrogel formation was evaluated at the appropriate time by photography.

sec.title: In vivo CDA release from CG/PF hydrogel
sec.p: The CDA or CG/PF (Cy7-labeled CDA) solutions were administrated by subcutaneous injection into the flank of C57BL/6 mice at fixed time points (days 0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25), and the accumulation of CDA at the injection site was measured using an IVIS imaging system (IVIS spectrum, PerkinElmer). To investigate the retention of CDA in brain tissue, 10 μl of CG/PF solution was injected into brain tissue and imaged by IVIS imaging system. Accumulation of CDA at the injection site was quantified by IVIS imaging system to quantify the fluorescence intensity and plot the drug release profile in vivo.

sec.title: Safety study of CG/PF in vivo
sec.p: Healthy C57BL/6 mice were intracranially implanted with CG/PF. At predetermined time points, mice body weight was detected. After 30 days of treatment, blood was collected for complete blood count analysis and serum biochemistry analysis. Major organs (heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney) were collected for H&E staining and histopathological evaluation to assess the safety of CG/PF.

sec.title: Establishment of in vivo orthotopic GBM model
sec.p: An orthotopic GL261-Luc tumor model was established in C57BL/6 mice using stereotaxic apparatus. After anesthesia with an intraperitoneal injection of tribromoethanol, mice were securely positioned in a digital stereotaxic frame. A midline scalp incision (5 mm) was created to expose the cranial surface. Stereotactic coordinates (2.0 mm lateral and 1.0 mm anterior to the bregma) were marked for burr hole creation using a precision drill. Subsequently, 2.0 × 105 GL261-Luc cells were intracranially implanted at a depth of 3.0 mm below the dura mater using a 25-μl syringe. After a 5-min stabilization period, the hole was sealed with bone wax and the skin sutured.

sec.title: In vivo orthotopic GBM treatment
sec.p: On day 7 postinoculation, GL261-Luc–bearing mice were randomly assigned to four groups. After intraperitoneal injection of d-luciferin (3 mg per mouse), real-time tumor monitoring was performed using the in vivo IVIS spectrum imaging system (PerkinElmer). For localized therapy, the original tumor implantation site was exposed, and 10 μl of therapeutic formulations was infused into the tumor bed using a 25-μl Hamilton syringe fitted with a 26-gauge needle. The therapeutic formulations were as follows: NS, PF, C/PF, or CG/PF (PTX, 100 μg per mouse; CDA, 10 μg per mouse; and GM-CSF, 2 μg per mouse). After 7, 14, 21, and 28 days of treatment, tumor growth in the mice was monitored using a bioluminescence imaging system. The survival of the mice was monitored daily after treatments.

sec.title: In vivo immune activation
sec.p: On day 7 after treatment, the cervical lymph node, tumor tissue, and spleen were collected to analyze the immune activation by flow cytometry (Beckman CytoFLEX). For cytokine analysis, whole-blood samples were processed for clotting at 4°C for 2 hours, followed by centrifugation at 5000 rpm for 10 min. The resulting supernatant was collected for subsequent quantitative cytokine analysis. For immune cells analysis, the lymph node, tumor tissue, and spleen were digested, filtered, and centrifuged, and acquired immune cells were counted and stained with corresponding antibodies.

sec.title: Orthotopic GBM resection model and treatment
sec.p: On day 7 after implantation of the GL261-Luc cells, well-established tumors had formed as evidenced by bioluminescence imaging, and the tumor resection was performed. Briefly, mice were anaesthetized with 3-bromoethanol and then secured in a stereotaxic apparatus. A midline scalp incision was made to access the preexisting burr hole. Tumor resection was performed using microsurgical techniques with blood aspiration using a vacuum pump. After resection, 10 μl of therapeutic formulations (NS, PF, C/PF, and CG/PF) were injected into the resection cavity using a 25-μl Hamilton syringe. Last, the wound was closed with tissue adhesive and the skin sutured. The postoperative immune microenvironment was characterized by detecting DCs, macrophages, CD8+ T cells, and Treg cells in the tumor tissue using flow cytometry.

The concentration of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-10) in the brain and serum was quantified using ELISA. Blood samples were collected from the mice at pre- and postsurgery time points, allowed to clot naturally at room temperature, and centrifuged at 4000 rpm for 20 min to isolate serum. After euthanasia, brain tissues were excised, weighed, and homogenized in saline. Cytokine levels in both serum and brain tissue homogenates were quantified according to the manufacturer’s instructions using commercially available ELISA kits.

Mice were considered long-term survivors if they remained tumor free for 120 days after tumor inoculation. Long-term survivors received secondary orthotopic challenge via contralateral striatal injection of 2 × 105 GL261-Luc cells at day 120. Naïve mice underwent primary tumor inoculation as control. IVIS spectrum imaging system was performed to monitor brain tumor growth on a weekly basis. Additionally, the behavior and survival of the mice were tracked following surgical resection and treatment.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (version 8.0). An unpaired Student’s t test was used for comparisons between two groups, and one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used for comparisons across multiple groups. Survival data were analyzed using the log-rank (Mantel-Cox) test. Data are reported as means ± SD. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05 (*P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, and ***P < 0.001).
